variants: most security tools watch the network or the process list, which made sense when the risky thing on a laptop was a person or a piece of malware. a coding agent running on an engineer's login looks like neither, since every command it runs is one that engineer is allowed to run. i think the moment before each step executes, on the machine itself, is the only place you can tell what the agent is actually trying to do.

a lot of engineering teams have already switched on the auto approve modes in claude code and codex, because clicking yes on every command gets old within a day. from then on the agent is reading files and running scripts with the engineer's own access and nobody is looking at the individual steps. i'd be curious whether your first deals come from security trying to rein that in or from engineering leaders who want cover to let agents run unattended.

i think agents make access controls a lot less useful, since an agent logged in as an engineer is allowed to do nearly everything it ends up doing. what matters is which file it opens and which command it runs next, and that's only visible on the laptop. how often do customers turn up agents they didn't know existed in the first week, and is that what gets the deal signed or is it the blocking?

most county emergency management offices are three or four people who write the plans and then run the eoc when something actually happens. that means the plan only gets a hard look when a state reviewer or emap asks for one, because there's no slow month to do it in. i'd be curious whether agencies come to you first for the plan reviews or for the questions they need answered mid activation.

a flood activation at a county eoc usually means someone needs to know what the plan says about opening a second shelter, and they need it now. the answer is somewhere in a few hundred pages of pdf, and the person who wrote that section is on the phone with the state. do agencies bring you in for moments like that, or for the plan reviews ahead of accreditation?

emergency management is a weird job where the person who wrote the hazard plan is also the one who has to execute it at 2am. offices that small can't keep a planner on document upkeep, so plans drift from the county they describe. i'd be curious which use gets an agency to sign, the crosswalk reviews or having the assistant on hand during a response.

most policy tools were built for government affairs teams at large companies, which already have a lobbyist in dc and someone reading the federal register every morning. a security company with a few hundred people usually has neither, even though one cisa requirement or a state ai bill can decide which federal deals close next year. i'm curious how often the first person using openpolicy at a customer sits in sales and not policy.

i think growth stage companies tend to notice policy only after it has already cost them a deal. a federal buyer asks about a new cisa requirement, or a state passes an ai law, and nobody inside saw it coming because it isn't anyone's job to watch. my guess is your first champion at most customers ends up being someone in sales and not legal, is that right?

the companies that need policy help most are the ones too small to have a government affairs team at all. a comment period opens on a rule that will shape their federal pipeline and closes without anyone inside reading it. i'd be curious whether the coalitions are what gets a company in the door, or whether it starts with the alerts and coalitions come later.

every team i talk to that pulls data off the web has someone whose real job is fixing scrapers. a site ships a redesign on tuesday, the pipeline returns empty fields for two days, and nobody notices until a customer does. with one shared api per site, a single fix covers everyone calling it instead of every team patching its own copy. i'd be curious whether people come to you for the speed and end up staying for the upkeep, or the other way around.

everyone building agents wants them to book, buy and fill out forms on the web, but almost nobody trusts a browser agent to do that unsupervised. it clicks through a checkout a little differently every run, and when it gets one step wrong someone pays for the wrong flight. a fixed call that does the same thing every time is something a team can actually test and sign off on. i'd be curious whether the action side is bringing in different buyers than the data side, or the same teams going further.

i think web data is one of those problems that gets harder with every site you add, because each one breaks on its own schedule and the upkeep never shows up in anyone's plan. i'd be curious which sites end up being the hardest to keep working and whether those are the ones customers care about most.

Most military satellites still book time on the same small set of Space Force antennas, and when two missions want the same pass somebody loses their downlink window. Opening that up to commercial antennas helps, but it turns scheduling into a buying decision across networks that were never planned together. Having SCOPe pick the window across both is the piece that makes the extra antennas usable. I'd be curious whether commercial operators are asking for the same thing yet or if it's still mostly a government problem.

I've heard a lot of satellite contact scheduling still comes down to people deconflicting requests days ahead, so a satellite that needs an unplanned pass waits in line behind the plan. Re-planning the windows every time something changes is a different job than building the schedule once. I'd be curious how much of the conflict resolution is still done by hand after SCOPe goes in.

I think ground scheduling is one of those problems that only gets noticed when it fails, because a missed contact means the data sits on the satellite until the next pass comes around, and for some missions that's hours. How do customers end up measuring SCOPe, by the contacts it adds or by the missed passes it avoids?

A voice agent can pass every scripted test and still fall apart on a real call, because the caller interrupts, mumbles an account number, or changes their mind halfway through. Testing it well means generating the calls you haven't heard yet and then checking live calls for the same patterns. I'd be curious how much of a typical customer's suite now comes from production calls versus scenarios the team wrote up front.

The scariest moment for a team running voice agents is swapping the model or voice provider underneath. A change that sounds better in a demo can break the insurance verification flow that nobody thought to re-test, and the first sign is an angry patient on the phone. I'd be curious how often a migration like that is the moment a team first comes looking for you.

I think the testing problem gets worse with every agent a company adds, since each one has its own flows, its own prompts and its own ways of failing on a live call. A team that could check one agent by listening to calls can't keep up across ten. I'd be curious how many agents a customer usually has running before they stop doing it by hand.

The big data vendors were built to label at volume with generalist contractors, and that model gets thin fast once the task is reviewing an LBO or a radiology read. Labs pushing into finance and medicine need people who have actually been accountable for those calls. I'd be curious how hard it's been to keep senior bankers and doctors engaged once the first project wraps.

A model that's right most of the time still can't go live at a bank or a hospital, because the one wrong answer is the one that ends up in front of a regulator. That's why I think the eval side matters as much as the training data in these verticals. Are customers coming to you more for training or for proof they can ship?

Grading answers works fine until the model has to actually do the job. A DCF can read clean and still have the terminal value wrong in one cell, and only someone who has built a hundred of them catches it. Putting bankers and physicians behind tasks with a checkable result is much closer to how that work gets judged. I'd be curious whether labs are asking more for the environments or for the expert hours.

Clinical trial billing seems like it should be simple until you see how a site actually gets paid. A coordinator logs an extra scan in the visit record, nobody maps it to the right line in the contract, and the sponsor never gets invoiced for it. I'd be curious how much of what you find in a first diagnostic was never billed vs billed and never paid.

I think site finance is one of those problems that gets worse with every study a site takes on, since each sponsor contract comes with its own budget, payment terms and amendments. Most sites deal with it by hiring another coordinator or just eating the revenue they can't track down. Which are pulling harder right now, the bigger networks or the independent sites?

CTMS tools were built to run the study and track visits, and getting the site paid was always someone else's job. So the money side ends up in a coordinator's spreadsheet, months behind the work. Pairing billers with software that reads the contract fills a gap the trial systems were never designed for. Do sponsors actually start paying faster once the invoices stop getting disputed?

Most DFIR firms are priced and staffed for the big breach, so a deep investigation only happens once something has already gone badly wrong. Everything smaller gets a quick look from the SOC and gets closed. I'd be curious whether customers are starting to bring you the incidents they used to just close out.

Incident response has always assumed an attacker moving at human speed, which is why a few days to scope a breach was acceptable. That stops working once attackers run agents that can go from a stolen login to a domain controller in an afternoon. A forensics team with its own AI underneath the analysts is built for that pace. Are you already seeing agent-driven intrusions in your caseload?

A company spots a strange login at 2am and calls its IR firm. Then it waits while someone scopes the job, requests logs and starts reading, and the attacker has usually had days inside by then. Getting to findings while the attacker is still in the environment changes what the customer can actually do about it. How often are you catching them before the data is gone?

Specialty drugs are one of the few corners of healthcare where the clinic buys the product before it knows it'll get paid back. An approved prior auth can still end in a denied claim over site of care or how the drug was sourced, and by then the infusion center is already out the cash. I'd be curious whether customers come to you for the auth backlog or for the denials they're eating after approval.

Most prior auth tools were built to get an approval number back and move on, which made sense when an approval mostly meant the claim would get paid. With specialty drugs that stops being true, since site of care, network status and benefit type can each sink the claim after the auth is done. Working the whole path from the referral fax to the appeal is a different product. I'd be curious whether infusion centers or specialty pharmacies are pulling harder right now.

The back office at an infusion center grows with every new biologic that comes to market, because each one brings its own payer policies, benefit checks and appeal rules. Most centers keep up by hiring more people to sit on portals and fax lines. Doing that work inside the EHR they already use means a center can add therapies without adding a coordinator for each one. I'd be curious how much of the volume still shows up by fax.

E-prescribing was built to send a script to whichever pharmacy the patient named up front, usually the one closest to home, before anyone knows the price or whether the drug is in stock. That holds up for most generics but breaks for telehealth patients with no local default and for expensive or short-supply drugs, where the first pharmacy is often the wrong one. I'd be curious whether customers first see the value in the reroutes or in the price shown before the script goes out.

A telehealth patient gets a new prescription, it goes to the pharmacy down the street, and two days later they find out it's out of stock or costs a lot more than it would a mile away. Then the clinic gets the callback. Showing price and stock before the script is sent, and letting the patient reroute it themselves, takes the clinic out of that loop. I'd be curious how often patients actually switch once they can see the options.

Being neutral seems like the hardest part of prescription routing to copy, since most of the companies that could show a patient price and stock also own a pharmacy or a PBM and make money on where the script lands. The platforms buying routing mostly want it to work across every pharmacy without anyone picking sides. I'd be curious whether neutrality actually comes up in the sale or whether customers mostly buy on fill rates and fewer callbacks.

For a PACE program the pharmacy bill is the small number. The big one is the fall or the hospital stay that follows a bad drug interaction, and the program pays for all of it. Pricing pharmacy against those outcomes with a performance guarantee is a very different conversation than a per-script contract. I'd be curious whether PACE directors already have the data to hold you to the guarantee or whether you end up building that baseline with them.

Most drug interaction checks still look at two drugs at a time, which made sense when the job was catching one bad prescription. A PACE participant on a dozen medications from several specialists has a risk that only shows up across the whole list, and nobody on the care team really owns the whole list. I'd be curious whether programs buy this as a safety tool or because they carry the cost when someone ends up in the hospital.

Hospice and PACE teams usually already have a pharmacy that gets meds out the door on time, so switching has to be about something the care team can feel. Fewer midnight calls for symptom relief and fewer interactions to untangle are the kind of thing a nurse notices in the first month. I'd be curious whether the first conversation is usually with the medical director or with the finance side.

Pharmacy systems were built to bill one prescription claim at a time and get an answer back in seconds. A flu shot or a strep test billed to a medical plan needs CPT codes, eligibility checks and denial follow-up, which is a different job, so most pharmacies either eat the denial or never bill it at all. I'd be curious whether independents or the regional chains are pulling harder now that the AI billing piece is live.

Pharmacists already give the vaccines, run the tests and do the med reviews. The money gets lost later, in medical claims that come back denied and never get worked because nobody at the counter knows how to work them. I'd be curious how much of what your customers recover comes from claims they were already submitting versus services they had stopped billing for.

Every new service a pharmacy adds, like testing or a med review program, brings a medical billing workflow the dispensing system can't handle. So the more care a pharmacy offers, the more it leans on one pharmacist who taught themselves CPT codes. I'd be curious whether that shows up first at the regional chains, where it turns into a staffing problem across stores.

Pharmacists in Ontario and BC can now treat minor ailments and prescribe, but the counter is still set up to fill scripts, so booking the visit, documenting it and getting paid all happen around the dispensing system. As more US states open up prescribing the same gap shows up there, with different rules in every state. I'd be curious how the US launches have gone so far and whether pharmacies there are moving as fast as they did in Canada.

With fewer people seeing a regular GP, the pharmacy counter has turned into the front door for a lot of basic care. The problem is that pharmacies run on software built to fill prescriptions, with nothing for booking a visit, documenting an assessment or billing for it. I'd be curious whether pharmacies sign up for the new revenue or for the front office time back.

Independent pharmacy owners usually don't buy on efficiency, since saved minutes don't fix thin dispensing reimbursement. What gets them to move is a service they can bill for that they couldn't before, which is why prescribing programs seem like the right way in. I'd be curious whether the phone line or the prescribing piece is what gets a pharmacy to sign first.

Most delivery networks were built for food and retail, where nobody has to prove who touched the package. A Schedule II script or a fridge item needs a signed chain of custody and the right temperature the whole way, which is why so many pharmacies still keep a driver on payroll. I'd be curious whether pharmacies come to you first for the controlled and cold items or for everyday volume.

Running your own driver works fine for one store, but it gets expensive fast once a pharmacy group adds locations or a telehealth partner starts sending scripts out for delivery. Each new site means another car, another schedule and another person to cover when someone calls out. I'd be curious whether multi-site groups or telehealth providers are pulling harder right now.

I think delivery is one of those things patients now just expect, but most pharmacies still treat it as a favor they do on the side. The cost hides in a tech's afternoon spent driving or in a courier who can't take a controlled script. I'd be curious whether the pitch that lands is cost savings or being able to say yes to every delivery.

Canadian dispensing systems were built as one server sitting in the back of each store, back when filling scripts was the whole job. Now pharmacists bill for MedsChecks, flu shots and minor ailments, so that work lands in a separate POS, a fax tool and a clinical app bolted on beside it. I'd be curious whether owners switch to you for the cloud piece or for having all of it in one place.

A fax comes in at 9pm, sits in the tray until morning, and then someone keys it into the dispensing system by hand before anyone can start filling. Reading the fax straight into a prescription takes out the slowest step in the day. I'd be curious how much of a typical store's volume still shows up by fax.

Switching dispensing systems is one of the scariest calls a pharmacy owner makes, since a bad week of migration means patients walk. That usually keeps the incumbent in place long after the product falls behind. I'd be curious what gets an owner to make the jump to you, and whether it tends to happen when they open a new store.

Most independents run on one primary wholesaler contract, and everything outside it gets bought by checking a few secondary suppliers one site at a time. On a shortage or an expensive brand the gap between suppliers can be big, but nobody behind the counter has time to shop it every day. I'd be curious whether pharmacies use you mostly for shortages or as the first place they check on everything outside the primary contract.

I think secondary drug buying is still one of the most manual parts of running a pharmacy, with price sheets, faxes and a handful of supplier sites to check before every order. I'd be curious whether the pull is bigger from independents or from long term care pharmacies.

Keeping it free for pharmacies and charging the supplier seems like the right call, since owners watch every dollar. The tension is that the primary wholesaler still wants as much of the volume as it can get. I'd be curious how owners end up splitting their buying once they're on the platform.

State licensing is one of those things that stays invisible until a distributor ships into a state where a rule changed last quarter. By the time anyone notices, product has already moved without the right license, and fixing it means dealing with the board instead of just filing a renewal. I'd be curious whether customers find you after a scare like that or when they're opening new states.

Licensing work has mostly been done by consultants who research the rules once and hand over a binder, which assumes the rules sit still until the next engagement. With every state changing requirements on its own schedule, that answer is out of date almost immediately. I'd be curious whether the evergreen piece changes how customers think about the services side of the business.

Every new facility, product type or state a drug company adds multiplies the licenses it has to hold, so compliance headcount tends to grow right alongside the business. I'd be curious whether customers point to the software or to your licensing team when they renew.

A patient picks up blood pressure meds every month at the same pharmacy and sees the pharmacist far more often than any doctor, but nobody gets paid to check whether the numbers are coming down. Medicare will pay for that work now, the pharmacy just has no billing setup or physician to sign off. I'd be curious whether owners sign on for the revenue or because they already feel like they're doing this work for free.

Pharmacy systems were set up around the money from filling scripts, with clinical care and its billing left to the doctor's office. Chronic care management pays for exactly the follow-up pharmacists are best placed to do, but only with a physician supervising and a clean claim. I'd be curious how much the IndyCare merger changed how fast a pharmacy can get going.

In a lot of rural towns the pharmacist is the only clinician a patient sees regularly. After a screening flags someone, the follow-up usually falls through the cracks because the doctor is an hour away and the pharmacy can't bill for it. I'd be curious whether the ACCESS Model changes how you prioritize rural pharmacies versus everyone else.

Wholesaler portals and pharmacy inventory systems were built for the normal week, where the contracted drug shows up on the truck. When it doesn't, the response falls back to spreadsheets, emails to the buyers and a pharmacist calling around, one site at a time. I'd be curious whether health systems buy you for the sourcing side or for coordinating substitutions with clinicians.

The cost of a drug shortage rarely shows up on the purchasing line. It shows up as a pharmacist spending a day finding an alternative, a clinician ordering something that isn't on the shelf, and three sites each solving the same problem on their own. I'd be curious whether system pharmacy leaders or site buyers are the ones pulling you in.

Shortages come in waves, which makes it hard for a hospital to justify a dedicated tool in the quiet months between them. The teams that need it most are usually the ones with the least time to set it up mid-crisis. I'd be curious whether the agentic work you're building is meant to make the product something pharmacy leans on every day.

Adherence software has been around for years and mostly told pharmacies which patients missed a refill, assuming the pharmacy could turn that into a billable visit on its own. Independents don't have the payer contracts, billing staff or medical group to do that, so the alerts just sat there. I'd be curious how much of the work you end up running yourselves versus the pharmacist.

I think pharmacy-run monitoring programs fit independents well because the pharmacist already knows the patient, and the payment is a flat monthly number an owner can actually plan around. That's a much easier conversation than most clinical services. I'd be curious whether hypertension or adherence programs are pulling harder right now.

Most independents have plenty of patients who'd qualify for a monitoring program and nobody free to make the monthly calls. Taking enrollment, devices and claims off the store means the pharmacist only does the part they're trained for. I'd be curious how many patients a typical pharmacy can carry before it needs to hire.

Most hospitals assume the price they negotiated with the GPO is the price they pay, but a contract that didn't load or a purchase that slid onto the wrong tier just becomes the new normal. Nobody has time to check every invoice against every contract, so it can run for months. I'd be curious which kind of miss shows up most often in a new customer's first month.

Wholesaler reports were built to show what was bought and what it cost, assuming the contract price loaded correctly. They'll tell you a price moved but not which contract should have applied. I'd be curious how the 340B report has landed with customers so far.

Every facility in a health system drifts on its own contracts and buying habits, so the bigger the system the harder it is to see who's paying what for the same drug. A miss at one site usually repeats at the others. I'd be curious whether system pharmacy leaders or the individual sites tend to bring you in.

A specialty pharmacy still gets a faxed referral, has a tech key it in, then spends the next week on hold with the payer checking benefits and prior auth status. Every one of those steps is slow, repetitive and exactly where a patient drops off. I'd be curious whether hubs or the pharmacies themselves are pulling harder right now.

Pharmacy intake was set up around a person typing each faxed script and a call center working the phone queue. That holds until volume spikes on a new therapy and the queue just gets longer. I'd be curious whether pharmacist edits are where the agents learn the most.

Pharmacies are understandably careful about letting anything touch a prescription before a pharmacist sees it. Keeping the pharmacist as the final check while the agent does the typing and the calls seems like the right line to draw. I'd be curious how long it takes a new customer to trust the intake enough to stop double checking it.

Dispensing systems were set up when the pharmacist's job ended at the counter, so assessments, prescribing and inspection logs ended up on paper or in a second system. Starting with one module seems smart, since few owners want to bet the store on a big migration. I'd be curious whether the manufacturer data side is becoming as big as the pharmacy side.

Inspections are one of those things a pharmacy only thinks about the week before the inspector shows up, and then everyone is digging through binders and printouts. Keeping the logs current as the work happens means that week looks like any other. I'd be curious whether the inspection piece or the clinical documentation is what gets a pharmacy to sign first.

A pharmacist doing a minor ailment assessment in Ontario often still writes notes on paper, faxes the doctor and re-enters the claim somewhere else. Multiply that by every consult in a week and it's a real chunk of a pharmacist's time. I'd be curious how the chains are rolling it out across stores compared to the independents.

Moving a prescription between two pharmacies on different software still means one pharmacist calling another and reading it over the phone, sometimes after sitting on hold. It ties up two licensed people for what's basically a records handoff. I'd be curious how many transfers it takes before a pharmacy stops picking up the phone for them.

A transfer network is only as good as the pharmacy on the other end, so the early work has to be getting enough stores on board that staff stop falling back to the phone. I'd be curious whether that's been spreading store by store or through buying groups and the software vendors.

Electronic transfers mostly work inside one vendor's network, which made sense when patients stayed with the same pharmacy. Now people move between chains, independents and mail order all the time, so the phone call is still the default across vendors. I'd be curious whether patient-started transfers are a big share of volume yet.

Pharmacies still spend a surprising part of the day on the phone confirming orders, taking card numbers and calling patients for insurance audits. Moving that to a text the patient can answer on their own time takes a lot off the counter. I'd be curious how the rollout across Revive's pharmacies is going and what you're seeing that a single store never would.

I think patient communication is one of the most underbuilt parts of pharmacy software, since most stores still lean on robocalls and a ringing phone line that pulls someone off the counter. I'd be curious what the roadmap looks like now that you're part of ReviveHealth, and whether it stays focused on independents.

Payers expect pharmacies to document patient contact for audits, and most stores still do it by phone and a scribbled note. Turning that into a questionnaire the patient fills out gives the pharmacy a record that holds up. I'd be curious whether the audit piece or the payment piece got pharmacies to sign first.

The C-II count at most independents still lives in a paper logbook, and a mistake usually doesn't surface until the DEA or a state inspector asks for the records. By then a miscount can mean a fine or a diversion investigation. Pulling dispenses and receipts in automatically keeps the count right every day instead of the week before an audit. I'd be curious whether owners come to you after a bad audit or before one.

Pharmacy systems were built to fill and bill, and wholesaler portals were built to order, so neither one keeps a running count of every Schedule II bottle across both. That gap is why the paper logbook is still around. I'd be curious whether long term care pharmacies or independents feel it more.

Tracking every controlled substance, and not only C-II, seems like the natural next step since diversion rarely sticks to one schedule. It also gives a multi-store owner one count across locations instead of a logbook in each store. I'd be curious whether the PLUS version is pulling in multi-store owners.

Card terminals were built for a store where you pay a fixed amount at the counter and walk out. A pharmacy fills the script before anyone pays, the copay changes by plan, and more of it goes out by delivery or mail where nobody's standing at a register. I'd be curious how much of a pharmacy's unpaid fills you're able to recover in the first few months.

A filled prescription that never gets picked up goes back to stock, after the pharmacy has already done the work and spent the time. Collecting the copay ahead of pickup with a link turns that into a sale. I'd be curious whether the delivery and mail order pharmacies or the retail stores feel that most.

Going through the dispensing system vendors seems like the right way into pharmacy, since owners rarely add a tool that lives outside it. The tradeoff is that the system vendor could decide to build payments itself. I'd be curious how you think about that as the partnerships grow.

Ontario pharmacists can now assess and prescribe for minor ailments, but most are fitting that into a shift built around filling scripts, with the forms and the differential done by hand. Walking the pharmacist through the assessment and writing the note makes it fit into a busy day. I'd be curious which provinces are moving fastest for you.

Pharmacists got a lot more scope over the last few years, but nobody gave them more hours in the day. Most of the time a consult takes goes to looking things up and writing the note, and the conversation with the patient is the short part. I'd be curious whether pharmacists end up doing more consults once the documentation is off their plate.

Kroll and Fillware were built to dispense and bill claims, and the clinical consult never really got a home in them. So the assessment ends up on a paper form next to the keyboard. I'd be curious whether the FillAssist version is how most pharmacies find you, or whether it's word of mouth between owners.

Generic CRMs assume a sales team working an outside lead list, but an independent pharmacy's best leads are the prescribers it already fills for. Those are the offices worth visiting, and most owners have no real way to track who they've seen or followed up with. I'd be curious whether owners start with the visit tracking or with the shared data across pharmacies.

Most independent owners know they should be visiting the doctor's offices that send them scripts, but between filling, staffing and payer calls it ends up on a sticky note. The owners who do it consistently tend to be the ones growing. I'd be curious how ATRIUMX has changed the way owners find you.

A shared data set across pharmacies is only useful once enough stores are in it that it looks like your own market. Until then owners tend to discount it and go with their gut. I'd be curious how many pharmacies it took before owners started trusting the numbers.

Most pharmacies have been treating DSCSA as a box to check, but the exposure shows up later, when a suspect product or a recall comes through and nobody can pull up where that bottle came from. Capturing it in the background from the pharmacy system means the record is just there when someone asks. I'd be curious how many pharmacies are still scrambling with the November deadline this close.

The first DSCSA tools were built for manufacturers and wholesalers with a compliance team and people who already speak EPCIS. A pharmacy receiving totes at the back door has none of that, so the work has to happen inside the dispensing system or it doesn't happen. I'd be curious whether buying groups have been the main way pharmacies find you.

DSCSA has a hard deadline, which is great for getting pharmacies to buy and harder for keeping them engaged once they're compliant. The receiving data is already sitting there, though, and it says a lot about expirations and overstock. I'd be curious whether owners have started looking at it day to day.

When a pharmacist calls in sick, the owner usually ends up texting the same three relief pharmacists they've used for years and hoping one says yes. If nobody does, the store either closes the counter or pays an agency markup for the day. I'd be curious how fast a shift typically fills once it's posted.

Relief staffing was built around agencies that vet a person and mark up every shift, which made sense when checking credentials took a phone call and a fax. Once licensure is verified in the app, most of what the agency was charging for goes away. I'd be curious how the US states have compared to Canada so far.

Staffing marketplaces have a hard time keeping the relationship on the platform once an owner finds a pharmacist they like. After the second or third shift together it's easy to just text each other directly. I'd be curious what keeps repeat bookings going through ShiftPosts.

Drug references like Lexicomp and Micromedex were built for the questions that already have an answer written down. The questions that eat a hospital pharmacist's afternoon are the off-label and formulary ones, where somebody has to go read the primary studies. I'd be curious how often a new question turns out to be one you've already answered for another hospital.

A P&T committee wants to know whether a cheaper alternative is safe to swap in, and a clinical pharmacist ends up spending a week pulling and reading studies on top of their normal shift. Most hospitals stopped staffing a dedicated drug information pharmacist years ago. I'd be curious whether the formulary work is starting to pull harder than the one-off clinical questions.

Every new approval and label change adds to the pile of questions a hospital pharmacy has to answer with evidence, while drug information staff keeps shrinking. I'd be curious whether health systems buy you as a replacement for a hire or as capacity they never had.

A clinical pharmacist who gets an off-label dosing question at 4pm usually has two options, go with what the reference says or lose the evening to PubMed. Most health systems cut their dedicated drug information role years ago, so that work just landed on whoever is on shift. Having a researcher pull and summarize the studies gets that pharmacist a real answer before the next round. Is the formulary and P&T work starting to outweigh the bedside questions?

Lexicomp and Micromedex are great when the answer is already written down. The questions that eat a pharmacist's afternoon are the ones where somebody has to read three trials and decide what they mean for one patient. Doing that research for them, and keeping it for the next hospital that asks, gets better with every system you add. How often does a new question turn out to be one you've already answered?

Every new approval and label change adds to the pile of questions a hospital pharmacy has to answer with evidence, while drug information staffing keeps shrinking. Handing those questions to a team that does the literature work means the clinical pharmacists stay on the floor. Do health systems buy you to replace a hire or to get capacity they never had?

When a pharmacist calls in sick at an independent, the owner usually texts the same few relief pharmacists and, if nobody bites, works the shift themselves. With store margins as thin as they've been, paying an agency markup for one day can wipe out the week. Letting the owner post the shift and have a licensed pharmacist grab it from their phone means the owner stops being the backup plan. Are owners booking further ahead now, or is it still mostly same day?

Inspections are something a pharmacy thinks about the week before the inspector shows up, and then everyone is digging through binders. Pharmacies are careful about letting anything touch a prescription before a pharmacist sees it. Keeping the pharmacist as the final check while the agent does the typing and the calls seems like the right line to draw. What does the first month look like before a new customer trusts the intake?

Pharmacy spend grows every year with specialty and biosimilars, but the purchasing team at most health systems stays the same size. The gap between what was negotiated and what was paid grows with it. Do systems usually expand you to more hospitals once the first site sees results?

Running the clinical program for the pharmacy gets stores live fast, but it raises the question of whose patient relationship it is a year in. Pharmacists who feel like a referral source tend to drift. How do you think about how much stays with your operators versus the pharmacist?

Cloud dispensing is a hard sell until something goes wrong with the server in the back. When it does, the pharmacy can't fill anything and patients start walking to the chain down the street. Do owners come to you after an outage like that, or when they open a new store?
